questions.stem: Which conditions must be present together for iron to rust?

options.text: Oxygen and water
options.explanation: Both ingredients are required at once, which is exactly what the three-tube control experiment demonstrates.

options.text: Water alone
options.explanation: The middle tube has water yet no rust, because the oil layer blocks the oxygen.

options.text: Oxygen alone
options.explanation: The right-hand tube has air yet stays clean, because the drying agent removes the water.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and heat
options.explanation: Neither is named as a rust requirement; the pair of record is oxygen and water.

questions.stem: Why is boiled water used in one of the control test tubes?

options.text: To remove any dissolved oxygen from the water
options.explanation: Boiling drives the dissolved air out, so that tube can withhold oxygen while still supplying water.

options.text: To kill any bacteria that might rust the nail
options.explanation: Rusting is a chemical process needing oxygen and water; bacteria play no part in the design.

options.text: To warm the nail so rusting speeds up
options.explanation: The point is removing a ingredient, not accelerating anything; the tube must show no rust.

options.text: To dissolve the calcium chloride faster
options.explanation: The calcium chloride sits in the dry tube; the boiled water belongs to the oil-sealed tube's design.

questions.stem: What is the role of the calcium chloride in the dry test tube?

options.text: It is a drying agent that absorbs water molecules present due to moisture
options.explanation: By soaking up every trace of moisture it withholds the water requirement from that nail.

options.text: It supplies oxygen to speed the rusting
options.explanation: The tube is meant to stay rust-free; the calcium chloride removes water rather than adding anything.

options.text: It sticks the nail to the tube's base
options.explanation: Fixing the nail is incidental; the design purpose is drying the air.

options.text: It colours the tube so the result is easier to see
options.explanation: No colour indicator is involved; the drying is what matters.

questions.stem: The middle nail sits in boiled water with oil floated on top. Why does it not rust?

options.text: The oil forms a barrier that stops oxygen reaching the water and the nail
options.explanation: With oxygen shut out, one of the two requirements is missing, so no rust forms.

options.text: The oil feeds the nail and keeps it strong
options.explanation: Oil does not nourish iron; it simply blocks the air from the water beneath.

options.text: Boiled water is too pure to react with iron
options.explanation: Purity is not the point; boiled water's job is lacking dissolved oxygen, and the oil keeps it that way.

options.text: The nail is a special rust-proof sample
options.explanation: All three nails are ordinary iron; the conditions, not the nails, differ.

questions.stem: Why does rusting eventually destroy a whole iron structure rather than just its surface?

options.text: Because rust flakes off the surface, exposing fresh iron below to rust in turn
options.explanation: Each flaked layer reveals new metal, so the damage eats inward and the structure weakens progressively.

options.text: Because rust strengthens the layer beneath it
options.explanation: Rust is soft and flaky; it protects nothing, which is why the damage continues.

options.text: Because iron dissolves evenly like sugar in water
options.explanation: The process is surface rusting that renews itself, not uniform dissolution.

options.text: Because the structure gets heavier and collapses
options.explanation: The failure is weakening from lost metal, not added weight; rust flakes away rather than accumulating.

questions.stem: Which set names common barrier methods?

options.text: Paint, oil, grease and electroplating
options.explanation: These four are the common barriers named, each physically separating iron from air and water.

options.text: Zinc bars welded to the surface
options.explanation: Zinc bars are sacrificial protection, a different prevention family from coatings.

options.text: Heating the iron until it glows
options.explanation: Heat is not a barrier; it changes nothing about air and water reaching the surface afterwards.

options.text: Storing the iron in salt water
options.explanation: Salt water supplies both requirements and would promote rusting, not prevent it.

questions.stem: What weakness do all barrier methods share?

options.text: If the coating is scratched or washed away, the iron is exposed and rusts again
options.explanation: A barrier only works while it is intact; any breach lets both requirements back in.

options.text: They only work in dry climates
options.explanation: Barriers work anywhere while whole; location is not the failure mode named.

options.text: They make the iron too heavy to use
options.explanation: Coatings add negligible weight; the real weakness is damage to the coating.

options.text: They react chemically with the iron and weaken it
options.explanation: Barriers are physical separations, not chemical treatments of the iron itself.

questions.stem: Why is a scratched paint layer worse than it looks?

options.text: Because porous rust lets air and water reach fresh metal underneath the break
options.explanation: The rust itself does not seal the wound; it conducts both requirements inward, so corrosion continues below.

options.text: Because paint poisons the iron at the scratch
options.explanation: Paint is inert to the iron; the problem is exposure, not poisoning.

options.text: Because the scratch makes the structure heavier
options.explanation: Weight is irrelevant; the issue is ongoing corrosion at and beneath the breach.

options.text: Because iron repairs its own paint layer
options.explanation: Iron does no such thing; the exposed spot keeps rusting until treated.

questions.stem: How does electroplating serve as a barrier method?

options.text: It deposits a thin protective metal layer over the iron, keeping air and water off
options.explanation: The plated layer is a physical coat like paint, but made of metal applied by electrolysis.

options.text: It removes oxygen from the iron's surface permanently
options.explanation: Nothing removes oxygen permanently; the plating simply stands between the iron and the air.

options.text: It converts the iron into stainless steel
options.explanation: Alloying would change the metal itself; electroplating adds a layer on top instead.

options.text: It magnetises the surface so water slides off
options.explanation: Magnetism plays no part; the plating works as a physical cover.

questions.stem: Which statement compares iron with some other metals under a broken coating?

options.text: Unlike some other metals, iron keeps corroding internally because its rust is porous
options.explanation: Some metals form tight protective layers, but iron's flaky porous rust leaves the metal below exposed.

options.text: All metals rust identically once scratched
options.explanation: The note's contrast says otherwise: some metals' layers protect, while iron's rust does not.

options.text: Other metals rust faster because they are heavier
options.explanation: Mass is not the driver; the difference lies in whether the corrosion product seals the surface.

options.text: Iron is the only metal that ever corrodes
options.explanation: Corrosion is general to metals; rusting is the specific case of iron, as the exam hint stresses.

questions.stem: Why is zinc chosen as the sacrificial metal for iron?

options.text: Because zinc is more reactive than iron and loses its electrons more easily
options.explanation: Higher reactivity means preferential oxidation, so the zinc corrodes first and the iron survives.

options.text: Because zinc is less reactive than iron and stays untouched
options.explanation: A less reactive partner would leave the iron to corrode first, defeating the design.

options.text: Because zinc is cheaper than any other metal
options.explanation: Cost is not the criterion named; the choice is grounded in the reactivity series.

options.text: Because zinc never corrodes at all
options.explanation: Zinc corrodes deliberately and must be replaced; that is exactly the sacrifice.

questions.stem: What happens to the zinc bars on a steel ship over time?

options.text: They corrode and must be replaced before they completely disappear
options.explanation: The zinc is consumed doing its job, so continued protection depends on timely replacement.

options.text: They last forever without maintenance
options.explanation: The zinc is being sacrificed continuously; without replacement the protection ends.

options.text: They transfer strength to the ship's hull
options.explanation: The protection is electrochemical, not mechanical; no strength is transferred.

options.text: They sink to the seabed once rusted
options.explanation: The bars stay attached while corroding; their loss is by consumption, not by falling off.

questions.stem: How is the zinc layer applied in galvanising?

options.text: By electroplating or by dipping the iron into molten zinc
options.explanation: Both routes coat the iron with zinc, which then protects it in two ways.

options.text: By painting liquid zinc onto the surface
options.explanation: Painting is a different barrier method; galvanising names the zinc coat applied by plating or dipping.

options.text: By hammering zinc sheets flat against the iron
options.explanation: Mechanical pressing is not the named process; plating or molten dipping is.

options.text: By heating the iron until zinc vapour settles
options.explanation: No vapour deposition is named; the two routes are electroplating and molten dipping.

questions.stem: What is ZnCO3's role in galvanising?

options.text: It forms when zinc reacts with oxygen and carbon dioxide in air, protecting the iron by the barrier method
options.explanation: The zinc carbonate layer is the coat's hardened outer skin, keeping air and water away from the metal beneath.

options.text: It dissolves the iron underneath the coating
options.explanation: The compound protects rather than attacks; its role is barrier, not corrosion.

options.text: It is the molten zinc used for dipping
options.explanation: The dip bath is metallic zinc; ZnCO3 forms afterwards on the surface in air.

options.text: It has no role; it is an impurity
options.explanation: The compound is the protective product of zinc's reaction with air, a designed feature of the coating.

questions.stem: A galvanised bucket is scratched deeply. Why does the iron still not rust?

options.text: Because the exposed zinc around the scratch still protects the iron sacrificially
options.explanation: The zinc beside the breach is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes in the iron's place even where the barrier is gone.

options.text: Because the scratch closes itself as the metal cools
options.explanation: Metals do not self-heal scratches; the protection comes from the zinc's chemistry.

options.text: Because the bucket is also painted underneath
options.explanation: No second coating is needed in the explanation; zinc's sacrifice suffices.

options.text: It does rust, because galvanising stops working once scratched
options.explanation: That describes plain barrier coatings; galvanising keeps protecting through its sacrificial action.
